text: Abdiel Leaves Alone: When Everyone Agrees, On What Grounds Can One Person Still Say No?
Satan does not announce rebellion at the outset.
First, he summons the angels under his command by night.
Ostensibly, they are to prepare to welcome the Son, newly proclaimed king.
The order passes down the existing hierarchy.
Countless angels leave their stations and come to the north.
They know Satan's leadership and believe this gathering belongs to their shared order.
Only when everyone has assembled does Satan change the question.
He asks:
We were free and noble. Why must we now bend the knee to another?
Ranks may exist, but freedom should be equal.
Who has the right to become king over equals and issue commands to angels who needed no laws and would commit no wrong?
He speaks of freedom.
Equality.
Resistance to submission.
He also asks his listeners to understand themselves anew.
The speech goes on for a long time without interruption.
Until Abdiel rises.
This scene can easily be told as follows:
When everyone is wrong, a brave person should believe in himself.
Paradise Lost does indeed praise Abdiel without equivocation.
The narrator says that among countless unfaithful angels, he alone remains faithful.
Neither numbers, example, fear, nor the mockery around him turns him from what he recognizes as truth.
The next day, he returns to the heavenly host still loyal to God, where he receives cheers and God's public praise.
The work has already told its readers:
Abdiel is on the right side.
But for people in the real world, “he was later proved right” is not the hardest part.
The real difficulty comes before the proof arrives.
When all the familiar people around you accept the same account, on what grounds can you still say:
You are wrong?
Majority opinion is not meaningless.
If many people capable of judgment, with access to similar facts, independently reach the same conclusion, that should usually prompt an individual to reexamine their own view.
Others may see what one has missed.
A shared tradition may also preserve experience that no individual could rediscover alone.
So “everyone thinks so” can be important evidence.
The problem is that it cannot do the individual's judging for them.
Nor has the unanimity Abdiel faces been formed through every angel's independent examination.
They first assemble under Satan's orders.
They then respond amid the same speech and language of identity, under one another's gaze.
When a group hears together:
Those who truly know themselves will not bend the knee,
Disagreement is no longer merely disagreement with a political judgment.
It may also look like a failure to understand one's own freedom and dignity.
Numbers quickly acquire a new force:
If no one has objected, does my doubt merely show that I am slow to understand?
Abdiel does not answer, “I alone disagree, so I must be right.”
He begins with argument.
Satan says the angels seem always to have existed and do not remember being created, so no one has a natural right to rule them.
Abdiel replies:
You cannot conclude that there is no creator merely because you do not remember your beginning.
Nor can you treat the Son as a member entirely equal to ordinary angels, then invoke equality against his rule.
He draws on divine order, the relationship of creation, and long experience within Milton's poem.
Modern readers may not accept his theological premises.
But his way of judging still deserves attention:
He does not make his isolation a reason.
Nor does he merely say that he feels uncomfortable.

He tries to expose the leaps in the other's argument: from “we do not remember being created” to “therefore we are self-created,” and from “we all have freedom” to “therefore any higher authority is illegitimate.”
A valuable objection cannot rest on sincerity alone.
Sincere people make mistakes too.
Someone can cling to a misunderstanding with immense courage, or treat every objection as group oppression and thus never allow facts to reach them.
So a minority position is not inherently noble.
It may satisfy another desire:
I see more clearly than everyone else.
Everyone's opposition only proves how exceptional I am.
In that case, isolation becomes evidence that cannot be refuted.
Few supporters mean that truth has a hard path.
Many critics mean that the world has been deceived.
Every outcome only strengthens conviction.
Abdiel is more than stubborn precisely because the work lets him genuinely answer the other's reasons.
He does not use the label of loyalty to suppress the question simply because Satan invokes “freedom.”
He explains the kind of order he believes can coexist with freedom, and accepts the possible consequences of arguing in public.
Of course, within Milton's universe, Abdiel's circumstances include things that dissenters in reality usually lack.
God truly exists.
Truth has an omniscient final witness.
God later praises him personally.
The narrator also tells readers at the time that Satan's argument springs from pride and envy.
We are not in the same position.
A dissenter in reality does not see a golden cloud confirming his position the next day.
Nor will the majority always plainly belong to a rebellious heavenly host.
That is precisely why the story cannot be reduced to:
Even if the whole world says you are wrong, just believe in yourself.
Abdiel's divine confirmation is a fact of this work.
It cannot be transplanted into reality as hidden proof possessed by every solitary person.
On what grounds, then, can a person in reality oppose the majority?
Not being few in number.
Nor feeling strongly.
At least several harder conditions are needed.
Do they understand the majority's strongest reasons, rather than oppose only its weakest version?
Can they explain what they rely on and allow those grounds to be examined?
Are they willing to acknowledge that they may be wrong?
If their judgment is mistaken, who will bear the consequences?
Do they dismiss everyone as ignorant because the group disagrees, or still regard them as people who can be persuaded and who can, in turn, persuade the dissenter?
Abdiel's scene offers no complete method for reality.
But it makes one thing clear:
Shared agreement does not exempt the individual from these questions.
I cannot say:
Everyone is doing it, so I need no longer judge.
Nor does Abdiel suddenly turn and leave.
First, he tries to stop the rebellion.
He urges Satan to seek forgiveness while there is still time.
He points out that rebellion will draw all its participants into punishment.
Only when Satan refuses and responds with new threats does Abdiel say that he is not fleeing on Satan's advice or under his intimidation, but leaving tents already dedicated to destruction.
His withdrawal is no casual “this place isn't for me.”
It means leaving former companions, a leader, his place in the hierarchy, and the whole world around him.
He will pass alone through hostility and mockery.
Not knowing how he will be received on the other side.
At that moment, leaving is both a judgment and a cost.
When is a person entitled to leave a community?
If people withdrew whenever they disagreed, any group would struggle to sustain cooperation.
Shared life already requires people to accept some decisions for which they did not vote.
It also requires them, when they lose, first to try to explain, correct, and shoulder responsibility, rather than forever seek a place where people only agree with them.
Abdiel offers no universal license for a dissatisfied minority to withdraw.
He believes the community before him is changing its fundamental allegiance and preparing an armed rebellion against the authority he regards as the highest order.
From his position, staying no longer means tolerating ordinary disagreement, but participating in an undertaking he considers fundamentally wrong.
The right to leave depends on what the conflict touches and what staying means.
More strikingly, his departure can be named in two ways.
To the loyal heavenly host, he refuses rebellion.
To Satan, he is a fugitive and an instigator of opposition.
The same action can be called loyalty or betrayal.
This shows that a community cannot be defined solely by its current majority.
If the group before him says:
We are the whole shared order. Leaving us means betraying everything,
It acquires a monopoly on deciding who is entitled to be loyal.
Abdiel maintains instead that his loyalty to a deeper order is precisely why he must leave his present companions.
This claim may be valid, or it may be abused by anyone causing a split.
So we cannot look only at whether he stays.
We must also ask what he is loyal to, how he explains it, and what responsibility he is willing to bear for the consequences of his actions.
At the beginning of Book 6, Abdiel has walked alone all night.
Dawn comes, and he sees the loyal heavenly host already drawn up for battle.
They cheer, because among the countless angels who left, at least one has not been lost.
The divine voice praises him for having fought a better battle alone:
First confronting the rebels with words.
Enduring universal blame.
Seeking only God's approval, even if the whole world considers him perverse and wrong.
This confirmation completes the work's own judgment.
But it may also make readers forget that Abdiel had not yet heard these words when he left.
Courage comes before reward.
If someone objects only when they know that history will vindicate them and the right camp will welcome them, they are taking a much smaller risk.
True dissent refuses to make numbers the final answer even while the outcome remains unsettled.
But divine confirmation raises another question in the opposite direction.
Abdiel knows that God exists and believes that God is omniscient.
His independent judgment thus ultimately rests on a supreme authority.
He is not someone who, in the modern sense, opposes all hierarchy and obeys only individual conscience.
On the contrary, he believes that true freedom lies in obedience to the most legitimate rule.
Satan uses the language of equality and resistance to enslavement.
Abdiel defends kingship and the order of creation.
Extracting only “bravely opposing the majority” would erase the substance of their dispute, even turning Abdiel into a character he himself would not recognize.
The structure can speak to the present.
Their actual positions must not be quietly replaced.
This also reminds us not to judge a side merely by familiar words of approval.
Freedom, equality, and self-knowledge can all be real values.
Satan's use of these words does not make the words themselves bad.
Loyalty, order, and service can also be real values.
Abdiel's use of these words does not automatically make every act of obedience right.
The question is what each word explains within particular relationships.
Is equality being used to deny real responsibilities and origins?
Is order being used to exempt power from explaining itself?
Does freedom leave everyone room to judge?
Does loyalty require people to participate in actions they believe are wrong?
Judgment cannot be completed merely because one side uses words that sound more modern and appealing.
Abdiel later takes part in the war.
He does more than preserve a mild dissent: after leaving, he joins the loyal heavenly host in using force against the rebels.
On the battlefield, he faces Satan again.
He says that he once stood alone against everyone, apparently in error, and that now his opponent will finally learn:
Sometimes thousands upon thousands can be wrong, and a few may know.
Then he strikes Satan first.
This prevents the story from being written as a pure hymn to peaceful expression.
When argument fails, the work moves into war.
Abdiel believes that those on the side of truth have the right to defeat by force those who refuse reason.
This part may not transfer directly into the everyday ethics of dissent.
But it cannot be cut away merely to preserve a hero suited to the present.
A minority can also leap from “I am right in the argument” to “therefore I have the right to force everyone else.”
In Abdiel's theological world, an omniscient God confirms and initiates a just war.
In reality, people usually have no such certain authorization.
So independent judgment must be distinguished from the limits of action.
A person has a right to say no.
A right to leave.
That does not mean that personal conviction alone grants a right to use any means against the majority.
Dissent protects the individual from being swallowed up by numbers.
It must also prevent the individual from turning personal conviction into a new power exempt from collective scrutiny.
When everyone agrees, on what grounds can one person say no?
Paradise Lost first answers:
Truth is not decided by numbers.
But that statement needs its other half:
Being few does not decide truth either.
Abdiel is not right because he is isolated.
He is right because the work judges his reasons, the object of his allegiance, and his loyalty to be right.
For those of us without an omniscient narrator, the only course is not to imitate his certainty, but to imitate his refusal to entrust certainty to the crowd.
The majority deserves a hearing.
So does the minority.
In the end, we must still return to facts, reasons, consequences, and the possibility of revision.
When Abdiel leaves, no companion follows.
No one applauds him.
There is only hostility and mockery around him.
He turns away nonetheless.
This scene deserves to remain, not because solitude is noble in itself.
But because any true community must allow a possibility:
The direction everyone is taking together may still be wrong.
A person cannot attain truth merely by opposing everyone alone.
But neither can everyone's agreement strip that person of the right to keep judging and refuse to participate.
Abdiel's departing figure makes unanimity something short of a final answer.
Among everyone’s “yes,” it preserves a place where someone can still say “no.”

*Textual basis: John Milton, Paradise Lost, Books 5 and 6 of the 1674 twelve-book edition. In Book 5, Satan summons the northern angels in the name of welcoming the new king, then questions the Son's kingship in the language of freedom, equality, self-creation, and refusal to bend the knee (approximately 5.657–802). After his speech has gone unanswered for a long time, Abdiel rises to refute it through the relationship of creation, experience, and divine order, and urges him to turn back while there is time (approximately 5.803–889). When Satan refuses, Abdiel leaves the camp alone through universal mockery. The narrator calls him the only faithful one among countless unfaithful angels, whom neither numbers, example, nor fear could turn aside (approximately 5.890–907). In Book 6, he returns to the loyal heavenly host and receives God's public praise; later, before battle, he says that sometimes a few may know while thousands upon thousands are wrong, and then joins the fighting (approximately 6.1–40, 6.111–189). This essay does not modernize Abdiel into an opponent of hierarchy, nor infer from the work's divine confirmation of him that a minority position in reality automatically proves itself right.*
